samples.summary: No test that the hook leaves focus alone OUTSIDE an opted-in toolbar — the scoping mechanism is entirely uncovered
samples.evidence: The fixture ToolbarMarkup() puts every focusable control (buttons, input, dropdown) inside the single <div data-canvas-toolbar="">; the only element outside is a non-focusable <div data-testid="canvas" /> (line 60). No test ever focuses a button outside the opted-in root. Consequently both scoping checks in the implementation — e.target.closest(TOOLBAR_SELECTOR) === null in onFocusIn (toolbar-focus-release.ts:106) and el.closest(TOOLBAR_SELECTOR) !== null in isReleasable (toolbar-focus-release.ts:66) — could be deleted and this suite plus src/app/slides/toolbar/index.test.tsx (whose only buttons live inside the opted-in <Toolbar>) would still be green. The hook installs document-level listeners, so losing the scope would blur every button on the page (thumbnail panel, side panels, dialogs). The opt-in attribute is presented as the design's safety boundary (module doc lines 22-25) yet has no negative test.

samples.summary: 'releases focus a closing picker hands back after a canvas click' does not exercise the path its comment claims
samples.evidence: The test fires pointerDown on the canvas and then calls trigger.focus() directly. In the implementation the pointerdown handler only does keyboardNavigating = false, and keyboardNavigating is already false at mount, so the fireEvent.pointerDown line is a no-op — the test reduces to 'programmatically focusing a toolbar button releases focus', which the first test already covers. No real modal Popover, no onCloseAutoFocus, no pointer-events-neutralised body is involved, so the 'dominant #882 path' described in the 6-line comment above it is not actually reproduced. It does still discriminate against an 'inside-toolbar pointerdown' gate variant, which is why this is minor rather than fully vacuous.

samples.summary: hasOpenPopup's two branches are never covered independently — the fixture sets both attributes on the same element
samples.evidence: The 'Text color' fixture button carries BOTH aria-expanded="true" AND data-state="open" (lines 43-45), and it is the only element the 'keeps focus on a trigger whose popup is open' test uses. Either half of the || in hasOpenPopup (toolbar-focus-release.ts:57-60) can be removed with the suite still green, so neither condition is genuinely tested. Only the negative for data-state ("on" on the Bold fixture) is covered.
searchedFor: grep for aria-expanded in the new test file

samples.summary: The role="button" branch of isReleasable has no test
samples.evidence: isReleasable accepts either el.tagName === "BUTTON" or el.getAttribute("role") === "button" (toolbar-focus-release.ts:68). Every focusable fixture in toolbar-focus-release.test.tsx is a real <button>; no element with role="button" on a non-button tag appears, and no test asserts a non-button, non-role element (e.g. a focusable div or a link) is NOT released. So both the added role branch and the tagName restriction that protects, say, a focusable contenteditable are unverified.

samples.summary: No test for the effect cleanup (listener removal / pending timeout clear) on unmount
samples.evidence: The effect's return removes the three capture-phase document listeners and clears the pending timeout (toolbar-focus-release.ts:120-126). Because the listeners are on `document`, a leak survives unmount and would blur toolbar buttons in every subsequently rendered view — a plausible and invisible regression. No test in toolbar-focus-release.test.tsx unmounts the Harness and then asserts a focused button keeps focus, and the Unhooked control renders in a separate render rather than after an unmount of Harness (so the control tests only pass today because RTL auto-cleanup happens to work).

samples.summary: The keyboardNavigating flag's stickiness (tab, then dismiss a menu with Escape) is documented but untested
samples.evidence: The implementation comment (toolbar-focus-release.ts:83-87) explicitly claims a user 'who tabbed to a trigger and then dismissed its menu with Esc keeps focus where they put it'. The only Tab test (test file line 159) tabs to a plain button and asserts focus stays; there is no test that tabs to the Arrange trigger, opens with Enter/Space, presses Escape and asserts focus stays on the trigger. That is the branch where the flag has to remain true across intervening keydowns, and it is the interaction that distinguishes this gate from a simpler one.

samples.summary: Test named 'marks its root' asserts the attribute is present anywhere in the container, not on the root
samples.evidence: container.querySelector(`[${CANVAS_TOOLBAR_ATTR}]`) matches any descendant. If the attribute drifted onto an inner group instead of the <Toolbar> root the test would still pass, even though the hook's scoping would then cover only part of the toolbar. container.firstElementChild (or the Toolbar's own element) would pin the intent stated in the test name.

samples.summary: Mobile toolbar branch: hook mounted but shell lacks the opt-in, and nothing tests that
samples.evidence: useCanvasFocusRelease() is called unconditionally (index.tsx:70) while only the desktop <Toolbar> carries data-canvas-toolbar (index.tsx:110); MobileSlidesToolbar does not. The new SlidesToolbar test deliberately forces the desktop branch via matchMedia (index.test.tsx:22-34), so the mobile path — where the hook is inert — has no coverage asserting mobile toolbar buttons keep focus.

finding.summary: No test that the hook leaves focus alone OUTSIDE an opted-in toolbar — the scoping mechanism is entirely uncovered
finding.evidence: The fixture ToolbarMarkup() puts every focusable control (buttons, input, dropdown) inside the single <div data-canvas-toolbar="">; the only element outside is a non-focusable <div data-testid="canvas" /> (line 60). No test ever focuses a button outside the opted-in root. Consequently both scoping checks in the implementation — e.target.closest(TOOLBAR_SELECTOR) === null in onFocusIn (toolbar-focus-release.ts:106) and el.closest(TOOLBAR_SELECTOR) !== null in isReleasable (toolbar-focus-release.ts:66) — could be deleted and this suite plus src/app/slides/toolbar/index.test.tsx (whose only buttons live inside the opted-in <Toolbar>) would still be green. The hook installs document-level listeners, so losing the scope would blur every button on the page (thumbnail panel, side panels, dialogs). The opt-in attribute is presented as the design's safety boundary (module doc lines 22-25) yet has no negative test.

verdict.reason: No test anywhere mounts useCanvasFocusRelease alongside a focusable element outside the opted-in `[data-canvas-toolbar]` root, so both scope gates (toolbar-focus-release.ts:107 and :69) are uncovered. The hook is mounted in exactly two test contexts: toolbar-focus-release.test.tsx, whose fixture places every focusable control inside the single opted-in div (the only outside node is the non-focusable `<div data-testid="canvas" />` at line 60, used solely as a pointerDown target at line 146), and src/app/slides/toolbar/index.test.tsx, which renders only SlidesToolbar and asserts focus on `Undo`, inside the opted-in `<Toolbar data-canvas-toolbar="">` (index.tsx:110). Neighbouring focus suites cannot cover it: tests/components/menu-focus.test.ts exercises releaseFocusToBody with the hook absent; tests/components/text-formatting/toolbar-focus.test.ts and tests/app/slides/toolbar/mobile-text-toggles.test.ts never mount the hook. Deleting either scope check keeps both suites green, since the remaining cases are excluded by the tag/role check, the keepalive selector, or hasOpenPopup. The hook installs document-level focusin/pointerdown/keydown listeners (lines 121-123) and the opt-in attribute is presented as its safety boundary (module doc lines 22-25), so this is a clear behavior with no meaningful test — major under the test-adequacy rubric.

finding.summary: No test covers the actual production wiring (`data-canvas-toolbar` + hook) on SlidesToolbar or BoardToolbar
finding.evidence: The new test file only mounts a hand-written `<div data-canvas-toolbar="">` harness (toolbar-focus-release.test.tsx:22-53). Nothing asserts that the real `SlidesToolbar` (index.tsx:110) or `BoardToolbar` (board-toolbar.tsx:186) renders the opt-in attribute or calls `useCanvasFocusRelease()`. If either mount regressed (attribute dropped, hook removed, `Toolbar` stopping its `{...props}` spread at ui/toolbar.tsx:22), every test in the suite still passes and issue #882 silently returns. The whole production surface of this diff is untested; only the hook in isolation is.

verdict.reason: A test covering the exact production wiring exists, co-located next to the component rather than under packages/frontend/tests. packages/frontend/src/app/slides/toolbar/index.test.tsx renders the real SlidesToolbar (line 55-59) and (a) asserts its root carries the opt-in attribute via the exported CANVAS_TOOLBAR_ATTR (line 63-66), which fails if index.tsx:110 drops the attribute or ui/toolbar.tsx stops spreading props, and (b) clicks the real Undo button and asserts focus returns to document.body (line 68-75), which fails if useCanvasFocusRelease() at index.tsx:70 is removed. The desktop branch is forced deterministically by the matchMedia stub (lines 24-35), and the file is collected by the runner via the src/**/*.test.tsx include in packages/frontend/vite.config.ts:268. For BoardToolbar there is nothing to cover: board-toolbar.tsx:131-139 documents that board deliberately does not opt in and board-toolbar.tsx:188 renders a bare <Toolbar>, so the absence of a board wiring test is intended behavior, not missing coverage.

finding.summary: The two Radix-dropdown tests (Escape close, menu-item select) may pass vacuously if focus lands on body naturally
finding.evidence: `expectFocusReleased()` only asserts `document.activeElement === document.body`. In jsdom, when a Radix `DropdownMenuContent` portal unmounts, focus can end up on `document.body` regardless of the hook (Radix's focus-restore-to-trigger relies on layout/focus behaviour that jsdom emulates imperfectly). If so, tests at lines 95-108 — the ones that model the actual #882 repro (Radix hands focus back to the trigger) — would stay green with `useCanvasFocusRelease()` deleted, i.e. fake coverage of the central scenario. A stronger form would first assert `document.activeElement === trigger` after close with the hook disabled, or assert the trigger was blurred (e.g. spy/`toHaveFocus` on the trigger before the deferred tick).

verdict.reason: The claimed vacuity is already neutralised in the same test file by an explicit negative-control suite. `Unhooked` (toolbar-focus-release.test.tsx:70-73) renders the identical Radix DropdownMenu markup without `useCanvasFocusRelease()`, and the controls at :185-194 (Escape) and :196-202 (menu-item select) assert `document.activeElement === trigger` — exactly the "stronger form" the finding says is missing. Because those controls run in the same suite, the finding's premise (jsdom leaves focus on `document.body` after the portal unmounts regardless of the hook) cannot hold silently: it would make the control tests fail and turn the suite red. Hence the hooked assertions at :122-135 are pinned against ambient behaviour and are not vacuous. The residual timing window (transient `body` before Radix's setTimeout(0) restore-to-trigger) is closed by RTL's async wrapper draining a macrotask at the end of each awaited `userEvent` call, consistent with the controls observing a settled `trigger` state. No over-mocking either: the real hook (:26) and real `releaseFocusToBody()` (menu-focus.ts:68-72) are exercised, with no `vi.mock` in the file. The finding also mis-cites lines 95-108, which are the "popup already open" and "pressed toggle" cases, not the Radix close paths it describes.
